title: The lottery winners
hookLine: we get used to good and bad fortune; a well-known lottery study was small but influential
carry: we adapt, often more than we expect

lines: THE NEW PHONE IS A MARVEL.
cards: The new phone is a marvel. The screen so bright, the camera so sharp. For a while.
Then one ordinary morning it's just the phone, with a crack in the corner, and a newer one is on a billboard. The same thing happens with a raise, a bigger apartment, a new town.
And, more surprisingly, it can happen with losses too. People get used to things. Researchers have a name for it, and one small, old study made it well-known.

teach.h: WINNERS NO HAPPIER, A STUDY FOUND.
THE INJURED, NOT AS LOW AS GUESSED.
teach.b: Philip Brickman, Dan Coates and Ronnie Janoff-Bulman interviewed lottery winners, people who had been seriously injured in accidents, and a comparison group of neighbors, and published it in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology.
The winners were no happier than the comparison group, and took a little less pleasure in ordinary things: chatting with a friend, hearing a joke, a compliment. Second, the other half.

The injured rated their present happiness lower than the comparison group, but not as low as one might guess. Researchers call this pull back toward where we started hedonic adaptation, sometimes the hedonic treadmill.

teach.h: SMALL STUDY; NOT ALWAYS ALL THE WAY.
teach.b: The study was small, and it has grown in the retelling. Researchers have kept testing the idea, and some argue that people don't always adapt all the way back; some losses can leave a lasting mark.
The careful version: we adapt, often more than we expect, but not always completely. Fourth, an old practice built on this.

teach.h: REMEMBER WHAT A THING REALLY IS.
teach.b: The Stoic teacher Epictetus told his students to remember what a thing really is, so it can't ambush them. Even when you kiss your child, he said, remember that you love a mortal being. It sounds bleak.
It's meant to do the opposite: to keep familiar things from going invisible. Adaptation dulls the good. Noticing can wake it back up.

how: Some contemplative traditions use deliberate noticing, such as giving thanks for ordinary things or the Stoic habit of remembering that what we love is passing, to keep familiar goods from going unseen.

o: learning new skills quickly when life demands it
getting used to gains and losses, more than we expect

games.q: you've just won the lottery. going by the study, how are you likely to be doing later on?
o: far happier than everyone, for good.
about as happy as your neighbors, and enjoying small things a little less.
games.why: the winners were no happier than the comparison group, and ordinary pleasures landed a little lighter. a small study, but the pattern of adapting has held up in part.

practice: Look around the room, or around your life, for something good that has gone quiet from being familiar: running water, a friend who always answers, your own two hands, the morning light.
Pick one, and look at it as if it had arrived today.

wordCard.voice: We adapt. Good fortune and bad both pull us back toward where we started, often more than we expect, though not always completely. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: we adapt, often more than we expect. Though not always all the way. Rest easy.
